## 2pg (2026-10-23) — how big is the DCN 3.1.2 hole? Measured: 5.3 % of the register map, and the scanout path is identical

The user, after 2pf: *"make it SHINE, make it DCN 3.1.2 so we get all the
things we need"*. Before writing any of it, measure the hole. All static, no
boot.

### What Apple actually ships

`AMDRadeonX6000Framebuffer`'s compiled source paths (strings):
`dc/dcn10` (9 files), `dc/dcn20` (12), `dc/dcn21` (2), `dc/dcn30` (9),
`dc/dcn302` (1), `dc/dml` (10), `dc/clk_mgr` (7), plus `falcon_dm` (30,
Apple's own display-manager layer). So `dcn302` is the newest generation
present - one minor version below ours.

Two personalities matter, from the kext's own Info.plist:

| personality | IOClass | category | score |
|---|---|---|---|
| `AMDGPUWrangler` | `AMDRadeonX6000_AmdGpuWrangler` | **IOFramebuffer** | **60000** |
| `AMDRadeonNavi21Controller` | `..._AmdRadeonControllerNavi21` | **ATIFramebuffer** | 1000 |

The Wrangler at 60000 would displace `.Display_boot` (IONDRVFramebuffer,
20000) outright. **And `RembrandtGPUPeer` currently sits in ATIFramebuffer at
65000, which would block the Controller** - a structural conflict of our own
making, and a one-line fix.

### The pivotal measurement: dcn_3_0_2 vs dcn_3_1_2 register maps

| | |
|---|---|
| shared register names | 5631 |
| **same offset AND base_idx** | **5332 (94.7 %)** |
| different | **299 (5.3 %)** |
| only in 3_1_2 | 771 |

And the differences are **not** in the scanout path:

| block | differ / shared | |
|---|---|---|
| **OTG** (timing generator) | **0 / 434** | identical |
| **HUBP** (surface fetch, the flip register) | **0 / 80** | identical |
| **CM** (color management) | **0 / 1000** | identical |
| **DSCL** (scaler) | **0 / 136** | identical |
| **DPP / OPP / DCCG** | **0 / 82** | identical |
| DCHUBBUB (memory hub / watermarks) | 74 / 77 | nearly all moved |
| MPC (multi-plane compositor) | 53 / 214 | |
| DC* (generic) | 91 / 295 | |
| AFMT / VPG (HDMI-DP **audio**) | 29 / 174 | |

Every register this project already uses is at the **same** offset and base in
3.0.0, 3.0.2 and 3.1.2: all ten OTG timing/status/frame-count registers and
`HUBP0_DCSURF_SURFACE_CONFIG`. `BL_PWM_*` exists in 3.0.0 but was renamed by
3.1.2 (rb_regs.h already carries the 3.1.2 location, 0x2f19).

**So Apple's dcn302 code would drive our timing generator and surface fetch at
exactly the right addresses**, and would get DCHUBBUB watermarks and MPC
blending wrong. That is a far better starting point than "write a generation",
and it is why this is worth attempting rather than declaring impossible.

### What is NOT just offsets

Honesty about the remaining work, because 5.3 % understates it:

* **DML** (`display_mode_vba_31`) is generation-specific *logic*, not offsets -
  different pipe/DRAM parameters. Wrong DML means wrong watermarks, which
  shows up as underflow and flicker rather than a black screen.
* **clk_mgr** - dcn31 talks to **SMU 13.0.x**; Apple's clk_mgr set is
  dce100/dce110/dcn10(rv1)/dcn21(rn). This is a real gap and touches the SMU,
  which is the user's decision territory.
* **ASIC identification** - Apple's tables must accept `0x1681` as a part they
  will build a controller for.

### A safer first experiment than expected

The Controller (`ATIFramebuffer`) and the Wrangler (`IOFramebuffer`) are
**separate personalities**, so they can be injected independently:

1. **Controller only.** DAL initialises and we learn how far it gets, while
   `.Display_boot` keeps the display - nothing displaces the working
   framebuffer. The risk is that DAL's `init_hw` touches registers during
   bring-up and blanks the panel; a reboot without the arg restores it,
   because the firmware re-initialises DCN every boot.
2. **Then the Wrangler**, which is the step that actually takes the display and
   the step that can make WindowServer hardware-composite.

xnu's fallback was already read in 2oz and applies here: if the Wrangler's
`start()` returns false, IOKit starts the next candidate in the category,
which is IONDRVFramebuffer. A clean failure is recoverable; a partial success
that programs the display wrong is the case to fear.

Headers vendored to `docs/linux-ref/` with provenance in `UPSTREAM.md`. Note
the prefix change - 3.0.x uses `mm<REG>`, 3.1.x uses `reg<REG>` - which made
the first comparison report near-total disagreement until it was caught
(rule 26, again).

## 2ph (2026-10-23) — a dry run of Apple's DAL on a DCN 3.1.2 chip, writing nothing

2pg said the hole is 5.3 % of the register map with the scanout path
identical, so Apple's DAL is worth pointing at this chip. Not blind, though: a
wrong DCHUBBUB write is an underflow or a blank panel, and 74 of 77 DCHUBBUB
registers moved. So this boot **writes nothing at all**.

**The choke point.** Every DAL register write in
`AMDRadeonX6000Framebuffer` goes through
`AMDRadeonX6000_AmdRegisterAccess::writeReg32`. Both overloads are defined per
`nm` and both are rule-2 clean (six pushes and a mov; no branch in the five
bytes Lilu overwrites). The hooks **record and drop** - `orig` is deliberately
never called. Reads are **not** hooked, so DAL sees the real chip and its
decisions come from true state.

One boot therefore yields the ordered list of registers Apple's DAL wants to
write to bring up a display on this chip, comparable offline against
`docs/linux-ref/dcn_3_1_2_offset.h`. That is the whole DCN 3.1.2 question
answered on the bench instead of on the panel.

**The interlock.** The danger is not the hooks, it is the hooks *failing* while
the controller still runs - then Apple's dcn302 code writes a DCN 3.1.2 chip
for real. So `AmdRadeonControllerNavi2::start` is routed too, and returns
false unless both write routes landed. No trace and no writes, rather than
writes without a trace. `dal_interlock 1` firing is a **good** outcome.

Rule 5 earned its keep twice here. There is no `AmdRadeonControllerNavi21::start`
- the personality's class inherits it, and only
`AmdRadeonController`, `...ControllerNavi` and `...ControllerNavi2` define it -
so the hand-written name was wrong until `nm` corrected it. And the
`AMDRadeonX6000Framebuffer` kext is in **SystemKernelExtensions.kc**, the same
collection as `AMDRadeonX6000`, which this plugin already injects successfully -
so the loading mechanism is proven, not assumed.

**Rule 2 refused one route.** `writeRegList` opens
`testq %rsi,%rsi; je ...` - a conditional branch at byte **+3**, inside the
patch window. That is exactly the 2gb pattern that panicked this machine twice,
so it is not routed. It reaches a vtable slot at +0x138 which was not resolved,
so if that slot is not `writeReg32` the trace will be short. **A suspiciously
small `dal_writes` is the first thing to check**, recorded here rather than
discovered as a surprise.

**Gating.** `-rbgpudal` gates both halves. The personality is injected in its
own match category `RBDisplayController`, deliberately - Apple puts the
controller in `ATIFramebuffer` where `RembrandtGPUPeer` sits at 65000 and would
block it, and a private category avoids touching the peer at all. It is
property-matched on `LoadDisplayController`, which the peer publishes only with
the arg, so without it Apple's framebuffer kext is never loaded and the boot is
identical to one without this code.

The one genuinely dangerous failure is both the write routes AND the interlock
route failing. `dal_wroutes` and `dal_srouted` say which landed; `dal_srouted 0`
with `dal_wroutes 0` is the case where DAL wrote real registers.

Keys: `dal_on`, `dal_wroutes`, `dal_srouted`, `dal_interlock`, `dal_start`,
`dal_start_ret`, `dal_writes`. The first 192 writes are logged with register
and value to `amd-log.txt`.

## 2pj (2026-10-23, boot 141) — both Apple personalities attach, and the read control earns its keep

`rbgpu-boot = 141`, loaded UUID matches the build (rules 8 and 15).

### What attached

```
RembrandtGPUPeer · AMDSupport · .Display_boot (IONDRVFramebuffer)
AMDRadeonX6000_AMDRadeonHWServicesNavi
AMDRadeonX6000_AmdRadeonControllerNavi21      <- Apple's display controller
AMDRadeonX6000_AmdGpuWrangler                 <- Apple's framebuffer
AMDRadeonX6000_AMDNavi21GraphicsAccelerator
```

**Both Apple display personalities attach and start cleanly on a Rembrandt
APU**, and `.Display_boot` survived - the private match category did exactly
what it was for, so the panel was never contested. `dal_start_ret 1` for the
controller.

### And the control is what made the result readable

`dal_reads 0` beside `dal_writes 0`. **A zero read count cannot mean "DAL chose
not to write."** It means that accessor was never touched at all - so the
instrument could not have protected anything, and `dal_writes 0` on its own
would have read as proof of safety. 2pi added that control precisely because
2ph flagged the ambiguity in advance; this is the one measurement in the
sequence that stopped a false conclusion.

### The register surface is wider than one class

`nm` shows four more paths in the same kext, all rule-2 clean:

| path | |
|---|---|
| `AmdRegisterAccess::hwReadReg32(uint)` | the low-level read |
| `AmdDalHelper::dalAtomReadRegister32(void*, uint)` | AtomBIOS read |
| `AmdDalHelper::dalAtomWriteRegister32(void*, uint, uint)` | AtomBIOS write |
| `AmdBiosParserHelper::readReg32(void*, uint)` | VBIOS parser read |
| `AmdBiosParserHelper::writeReg32(void*, uint, uint)` | VBIOS parser write |

There is deliberately **no** `hwWriteReg32`, so
`AmdRegisterAccess::writeReg32` really is the bottom of that path - checked,
not assumed. And the strings name **`dm_read_reg_func`**, so DAL's generic
register layer reaches hardware through a **function pointer**, which is why
routing the class methods alone caught nothing.

All five are now routed: writes recorded and **dropped**, reads **passed
through** and counted, with a separate counter per path (`dal_r_hw`,
`dal_r_atom`, `dal_r_bios`, `dal_w_atom`, `dal_w_bios`) because "which path
does Apple's DAL use on this chip" is the open question and one aggregate
number would hide it.

### The honest state of the experiment

The Wrangler is in a private category, which protected the panel **and**
probably prevented anything from driving it as a framebuffer - no
`enableController`, no `setDisplayMode`, so no reason for DAL to touch
hardware. That trade-off is why the dry run has not yet traced anything.

So the order matters and is deliberate: **prove the hooks fire before promoting
the Wrangler into `IOFramebuffer`.** If `dal_r_*` all stay zero with the full
surface routed, that is strong evidence nothing asks DAL to do hardware work in
a private category, and promotion becomes the only way forward - at which point
the dry-run protection will have been demonstrated rather than hoped for.
Promoting first would be writing real DCN registers with unproven
interception.

## 2pk (2026-10-23, boot 142) — the hooks fire, and the private category is the thing blocking DAL

`rbgpu-boot = 142`, loaded UUID matches the build.

```
dal_on 1   dal_wroutes 1   dal_srouted 1   dal_start 1   dal_start_ret 1
dal_r_hw 4        <- THE HOOKS FIRE
dal_reads 0  dal_r_atom 0  dal_r_bios 0  dal_w_atom 0  dal_w_bios 0  dal_writes 0
```

**Interception is now demonstrated rather than hoped for.** `dal_r_hw 4` is
four real reads through `AmdRegisterAccess::hwReadReg32`, so the routes land
and fire. And it names the path: of the six register entry points in that
kext, DAL used **only** `hwReadReg32` - not `readReg32`, not AtomBIOS, not the
VBIOS parser.

**Four reads and zero writes** with both personalities attached settles what
2pj left open: in a private match category, nothing drives DAL. No
`enableController`, no `setDisplayMode`, so no reason to touch hardware. The
safety that protected the panel is the same thing preventing the experiment.

### Two instrument fixes, one of which was load-bearing

**2pi's 2en throttle worked and was the prerequisite for everything here.** The
ring went from 506 of 512 entries from one log site to **90+ distinct milestone
tags**. Without it nothing below would have been diagnosable.

**But a ring is still the wrong shape for this trace.** `RBGPULog` keeps the
most RECENT 512 lines, and the DAL hooks run at the very start of boot, so the
accelerator's own bring-up logging evicted them - the trace was unreadable even
with the flood fixed. So the trace now has its own storage: chunked string diag
keys `dal_tr0..dal_tr15` (16 x 12 = 192 entries) in `RBGPUDiag`, which nothing
evicts. Each entry is `<kind><reg>=<val>`, kind being `w`/`W` for the two
writeReg32 overloads, `A` AtomBIOS, `B` VBIOS parser, `r` hwRead.

### Promoting the Wrangler, and why it must decline

DAL needs the Wrangler to actually BE the framebuffer. But promoting it is a
one-way door **if it succeeds**: Apple ships it in `IOFramebuffer` at 60000
against IONDRVFramebuffer's 20000, and with every write dropped it cannot
possibly bring up a display - so a successful `start()` would hand the panel to
a framebuffer that physically cannot drive it. Black screen, and rule 12 says
that is indistinguishable from a hang.

So the promoted path calls Apple's `start()` - DAL runs, writes recorded and
swallowed, trace captured - and then returns **false** regardless. xnu's start
loop is "start the best (until success) of each category" (read in 2oz), so the
false falls through to IONDRVFramebuffer. **Full trace and a working display.**
The promoted personality scores 30000, enough to win the category and be
asked, and it declines only when promoted - the private-category path keeps
boot 142's behaviour exactly.

If `AmdGpuWrangler::start` fails to route, the promoted personality could KEEP
the framebuffer it cannot drive. `dalfb_srouted 0` says so, and the remedy is
to remove `-rbgpudalfbreal`.

Keys: `dalfb_start`, `dalfb_start_ret`, `dalfb_declined`, `dalfb_srouted`,
`dal_tr_n`, `dal_tr0..15`.

## 2pl (2026-10-23, boot 143) — THE DECLINE PANICKED THE MACHINE. Returning false from start() does not undo what start() did.

Boot 143 panicked ~5.5 s in. The user rescued with `-rbgpuoff`. **This was my
error, and 2pk had already named it without mitigating it.**

```
panic(cpu 7): Kernel trap, type 14 = page fault
CR2: 0x0000000000000000      RDI: 0x0000000000000000      <- NULL `this`
RIP: AMDRadeonX6000_AmdGpuWrangler::vendor_doDeviceAttribute + 0xd4
  <- AppleGraphicsDeviceControl::vendor_doDeviceAttribute + 0x27
  <- AppleGraphicsDeviceControl::filtered_doDeviceAttribute + 0x1027
  <- AppleGraphicsDeviceControl::setDeviceAttribute + 0x1d
  <- AppleGPUWrangler -> IOInterruptEventSource::checkForWork
  <- IOWorkLoop::runEventSources / threadMain
System uptime: 5500804735 ns
```

### The mechanism

Apple's `AmdGpuWrangler::start()` **registers the Wrangler with
AppleGraphicsDeviceControl** - a different kext. 2pk let that start() run and
then returned **false**, reasoning correctly from xnu's "start the best (until
success) of each category" that IOKit would fall through to
IONDRVFramebuffer and keep the panel. The fall-through is real and did happen.

What is not real is the assumption underneath it: IOKit unwinds the
**attachment**, not the **side effects**. Our instance was detached and freed;
AGDC's registration survived; 5.5 seconds later AGDC's workloop called
`vendor_doDeviceAttribute` on the dead pointer and faulted on a NULL `this`.

**The reusable rule: returning false from `start()` does not undo what
`start()` did.** A cross-kext registration is a side effect, and there is no
hook that reverses it. This belongs with rule 13 and rule 20 - a success/failure
return describes the caller's bookkeeping, not the world.

And the process failure matters more than the bug. 2pk's own comment said
*"calling orig then returning false leaves Apple's objects half-initialised.
Could panic or leak. But it's bounded."* **Naming a risk is not mitigating it.**
The honest options at that point were to find the registration and block it, to
guard the entry points, or to not promote at all - and I took none of them
because the decline looked elegant.

### The fix

1. **The forced decline is gone.** The Wrangler's `start()` result is passed
   through untouched, the object stays alive, AGDC's registration stays valid,
   and the panic cause is removed. The cost is honest: when promoted, the
   Wrangler really does own `IOFramebuffer`. Every DAL write is still dropped,
   so the hardware is untouched and the firmware's scanout keeps running - the
   panel may well survive. If it does not, remove `-rbgpudalfbreal`.
2. **A guard on the same shape of bug by a different route.** Apple's own
   `start()` can fail on this chip and produce exactly boot 143's sequence - a
   freed Wrangler with a live AGDC registration.
   `vendor_doDeviceAttribute` is the **single** AGDC-facing entry point on the
   class (nm) and is rule-2 clean, so it is routed and refuses with
   `kIOReturnNoDevice` when `this` is not a kernel VA. Rule 19 exactly: a NULL
   check is not a pointer check, and `RDI 0x0` is what it would have caught.
3. **The DAL keys now persist to NVRAM** (`dal_writes`, `dal_r_hw`,
   `dal_tr_n`, `dalfb_start_ret`, `dalfb_grouted`, `dalfb_attr_blocked`).
   Boot 144 may come up with no usable screen, and without these in the
   512-byte NVRAM summary the boot would teach nothing (rule 14). The full
   trace stays in `dal_tr0..15` in `RBGPUDiag` and needs a readable boot - the
   NVRAM budget cannot hold 16 chunks.

## 2pm (2026-10-23, boot 144) — THE PROMOTED DRY RUN IS SELF-CONTRADICTORY. A hang, traded for a panic, from one impossible requirement.

Boot 144 never finished booting: Apple logo, progress bar filling slower and
slower, no panic. The user power-cycled and rescued with `-rbgpuoff`.

### What the evidence says, and what it does not

NVRAM was **useless and had to be read as such** (rules 8, 11, 12):

| | |
|---|---|
| `rbgpu-boot` | **142** - never incremented, so nothing in NVRAM is this boot's |
| `rbgpu-arm` | still `1` |
| `rbgpu-prog` / `rbgpu-gate` | `b=142` - stale |
| panic report | none newer than 09:56 - it **hung**, it did not trap |

The still-set arm *looked* like proof the peer never ran, and that reading was
wrong - rule 12 warns against exactly this. The unified log settled it,
because `/var/db/diagnostics` retains the previous boot:

```
10:02:29  kernelmanagerd: Could not find: Extension 'com.apple.kext.AMDRadeonX6000Framebuffer'
10:02:29  kernelmanagerd: Received kext load notification: ...AMDRadeonX6000Framebuffer
10:02:29  WindowServer [GPUWrangler] (reg) gpu 0xfbc7 vid.did=1002.1681
            agdc       0x000000000
            gpuc       0x1000004b0  /AMDRadeonX6000_AmdGpuWrangler
            agdpclient 0x000000000
            accel      0x1000004b6  /AMDRadeonX6000_AMDNavi21GraphicsAccelerator
```

So the boot got **as far as WindowServer**. The peer ran, published its
properties, and the Wrangler loaded and became `gpuc`. The arm's survival is
best explained by the forced NVRAM sync not reaching flash before a hard power
cut - which is precisely what 2dg records happening before.

**And the keystone, with a control (rule 26):** that registration has **no
`fb0:0` line at all**, where working boot 142's identical lines read
`fb0:0 0x1000004b2 /IONDRVFramebuffer`. There was **no framebuffer in the
system.**

### The mechanism, and it is a design error not a bug

Our promoted Wrangler won `IOFramebuffer` at score 30000 against
IONDRVFramebuffer's 20000. Its `start()` **succeeded**, because 2pl removed
the decline. So IONDRV never attached - and the Wrangler cannot drive a panel
with every register write swallowed. No framebuffer, WindowServer retrying
forever, progress bar crawling.

**One impossible requirement, two failures:**

* For DAL to do hardware work, the Wrangler must own `IOFramebuffer`.
* For safety, its writes must be dropped.
* A framebuffer that owns the display but cannot write registers has no
  picture.

2pk resolved it by declining -> **panic** (AGDC held a registration across the
free). 2pl resolved it by not declining -> **hang** (no framebuffer). Those are
not two bugs. They are the same contradiction, and I shipped it twice.

### The way out: drop only what is WRONG

`src/common/rb_dcn_deny.h`, **generated** by `tools/re/dcn_denylist.py` from
the two vendored headers - 299 dword offsets that moved between dcn302 and
dcn312. DAL then programs everything it can get right (the whole scanout path
is identical) and is blocked precisely where it would hit the wrong register.
A hosttest guards it and was checked to FAIL when broken: inserting
OTG0_OTG_H_TOTAL into the list trips both the sortedness and the
search-finds-its-own-entry checks.

### Why it refuses to arm, and this is the important part

The deny list is keyed on **dword offsets from the Linux headers**. What
`writeReg32`'s register argument actually carries on Apple's side - a dword
offset, a byte address, or an encoded id like the accelerator's
`(dword << 32) | hwid` - is **NOT established**. Applying the list anyway
would be the recurring error of this project in its purest form.

So `-rbgpudalpass` **refuses to arm** unless `rbgpudalenc=dword|byte` is also
given, logs the refusal, sets `dal_pass_refused`, and keeps dropping every
write. The units cost nothing to learn: boot 142's exact configuration -
controller only, no promotion, **display intact** - produced four reads, and
`dal_tr0` now captures them with their addresses. Four numbers settle it, on a
boot that cannot hurt anything.

## 2pn (2026-10-23, boot 143 recaptured) — THE UNITS ARE SETTLED, and 2pm's deny list was wrong in kind

`rbgpu-boot = 143`, loaded UUID `3BDD5711` matches the build. Controller only,
no promotion, **display intact** - the safe boot, as intended.

```
dal_on 1  dal_wroutes 1  dal_srouted 1  dalfb_grouted 1  dalfb_srouted 1
dal_start 1  dal_start_ret 1   dalfb_start 1  dalfb_start_ret 1
dal_r_hw 4   dal_tr_n 4   dal_pass 0   (all other paths 0)
dal_tr0 = 'rd31=ff70ff00 rde3=1000 rde7=100 rde8=80000 '
```

The evictionless trace channel worked. Both personalities started. And note
`dalfb_grouted 1` - the boot-143 panic guard is in place.

(The `dalfb_*` keys were nearly missed: a grep for `"dal_[a-z_]*"` does not
match `dalfb_grouted`, because there is no underscore after `dal`. Rule 26 for
the third time this session - the search is an instrument.)

### The units: raw dword offsets, BASE_IDX applied inside

Four reads, tested against **both** interpretations and this chip's real DMU
bases from `rbdump` (`0x12 0xc0 0x34c0 0x9000 0x2403c00`):

| | raw dword offset | absolute index |
|---|---|---|
| `0xd31` | `CM0_CM_GAMUT_REMAP_C21_C22` (base2) | nothing |
| `0xde3` | `CM0_CM_SHAPER_RAMA_END_CNTL_B` (base2) | nothing |
| `0xde7` | `CM0_CM_SHAPER_RAMA_REGION_2_3` (base2) | nothing |
| `0xde8` | `CM0_CM_SHAPER_RAMA_REGION_4_5` (base2) | nothing |

Four for four coherent one way, zero the other, and the values fit: `0xff70ff00`
is a packed pair of small negative 2.13 coefficients, exactly what a gamut
remap matrix holds. So **`reg` is the raw header dword offset** and the base is
applied inside the accessor. `rbgpudalenc=dword`.

### And that exposed 2pm's deny list as wrong in KIND, not just in count

2pm asked "which registers moved?" and keyed the list on offsets. **A dword
offset is not a unique register identity** - two registers with different
BASE_IDX share one. Measured: **98 of 2pm's 299 denied offsets were also the
offset of an UNMOVED register**, so that list would have blocked correct
writes, e.g. `DCHUBBUB_ARB_DF_REQ_OUTSTAND` (moved) sharing `0x505` with
`MPC_CRC_RESULT_GB` (unmoved).

The right question is per-base: **for BASE_IDX 2, does a dcn302 write to
offset O land on the same register in dcn312?** Three outcomes:

| | |
|---|---|
| same register - ALLOW | 3957 offsets (the whole scanout path) |
| nothing in dcn312 - write is a no-op | 1151 offsets |
| **a DIFFERENT real register - DENY** | **160 offsets** |

160, not 299, and a different 160. The entries show why it matters:
`0x089` is `DOMAIN4_PG_STATUS` to dcn302 and `DOMAIN16_PG_CONFIG` here - DAL
reading a power-gate status would **write a power-gate config for the wrong
domain**. That is the class of damage this list exists to stop.

The generator now takes `danger` (the 160, default) or `all` (plus the 1151,
which costs DAL ~23 % of its base-2 writes and will very likely make it fail -
a diagnostic setting, not a working one).

**KNOWN LIMITATION, recorded now rather than discovered later:** BASE_IDX 2
only - 5268 of 6402 registers, and where 4 of 4 observed accesses went.
BASE_IDX 3 (977 registers, overwhelmingly HDMI/DP audio: AFMT, VPG, DIG) has
**71** dangerous offsets of its own and is **not covered**, because which
argument of `writeReg32(reg, val, uint8, uint)` carries the base is still
unestablished. Audio is not needed for first light.

The hosttest was re-anchored on measured data and verified to FAIL when the
data is wrong - removing the `0x089` entry trips it.

## 2po (2026-10-23, boot 145) — NEGATIVE RESULT: Apple's dcn302 DAL cannot bring up DCN 3.1.2 by filtering writes. DCHUBBUB is why.

Boot 145 hung exactly as boot 144 did - logo, bar crawling, no panic - with
the selective pass-through **armed** (`-rbgpudalpass rbgpudalenc=dword` both
confirmed present in boot-args).

Evidence, and the limits of it:

* `rbgpu-boot` still **143** (rule 8), so every NVRAM value is stale - the
  `dal_writes=0 dal_r_hw=4 dal_tr_n=4` read out of it is boot 143's.
* No panic report. Unified log reached WindowServer at 10:38:47 and kept
  logging for ~35 s before going quiet.
* And the same keystone as 144, with the same control: AppleGPUWrangler's
  registration has `gpuc /AMDRadeonX6000_AmdGpuWrangler`, `accel
  /...GraphicsAccelerator`, and **no `fb0:0` line** - no framebuffer.
* Our own `2pm:`/`2pj:` log lines reach neither the unified log nor a readable
  ring, so **there is no direct trace of what DAL wrote.** That is a real gap,
  not a conclusion.

### Why it cannot work, measured

What the 160-entry deny list actually blocks:

| | |
|---|---|
| **DCHUBBUB** | **46** |
| SURFACE / VTG / MMHUBBUB / WBIF | 22 |
| power-gating domains | 11 |
| everything else | 81 |

**DCHUBBUB dominates, and 2pg measured 74 of its 77 registers as having
moved** - almost the entire block relocated between dcn302 and dcn312.
DCHUBBUB is the display memory hub: it arbitrates DRAM requests for scanout.
Without it programmed, the pipe has timing but cannot fetch pixels.

So both branches fail, and not by accident:

* **Deny** the 46 -> DAL cannot program the data path, waits on a hub that
  never becomes ready, burns `generic_reg_wait` timeouts. That is exactly the
  "slower and slower" symptom, twice.
* **Pass** the 46 -> dcn302 offsets land on different dcn312 registers.

**The one block that relocated almost entirely is the one block you cannot
skip.** 2pg's headline - 94.7 % of registers identical, scanout path
bit-identical - was true and *misleading*: the 5.3 % that differs is
concentrated precisely in the bring-up path, and a percentage is not a
difficulty measure when the remainder is load-bearing.

### What this closes, and what it does not

**Closed: write filtering.** No deny/allow policy over a shared address space
can reconcile dcn302 code with dcn312 hardware, because the mismatch is
topological (which register is where, how many power domains, how the hub is
organised), not a set of typos. Three boots said so three ways - 2pk's panic,
2pm's hang, 2po's hang - and the static measurement explains all three.

**Still open, and honestly a long shot:** *remapping* instead of blocking -
rewriting a dcn302 offset to wherever that same register NAME lives in
dcn312. Feasible to generate from the two headers. But DCN 3.1 changed
DCHUBBUB's *semantics* as well as its addresses (detile-buffer segmentation,
different watermark encodings), so correctly-addressed writes would still
carry dcn302-shaped VALUES - the DML problem 2pg already flagged as "not just
offsets". Addresses are the easy half.

### Process note

I told the user `dal_passed` and `dal_denied` would persist to NVRAM so a
failed boot would still say how far DAL got. **They were never in the key
list** - 2pl added `dal_writes`, `dal_r_hw`, `dal_tr_n`,
`dalfb_start_ret`, `dalfb_grouted`, `dalfb_attr_blocked` and no more. So boot
145 could not answer the one question it was spent on. Added now, but the
lesson is the recurring one: **state what makes a reading possible before
spending the boot that depends on it.**

---

## 2pp (2026-10-23) — the accelerator is ALREADY bound to the framebuffer, and the flip window is 8 MB. Zero boots.

The user asked whether the accelerated framebuffer is dead and whether
DCHUBBUB can be got past or reprogrammed. The answer to the second is **it
never needed reprogramming**, and the answer to the first is **no** — because
the premise of 2ph–2po was wrong in a way that is measurable from static data
and a capture already on disk.

### DCHUBBUB never needed to be touched

2ph–2po tried to make Apple's **dcn302** DAL perform a **full modeset** on
dcn312 hardware. A modeset reprograms every block from scratch, which is why
DCHUBBUB — 46 of the 160 denied offsets, 74 of 77 registers relocated — became
load-bearing. But the firmware **already programmed DCHUBBUB** and it is
working: `OTG0_CONTROL = 0x00011201`, DMCUB 4.0.15.47, 1920x1080 scanning out
of MC `0xf400000000` at 143.833 Hz, right now, on the machine the user is
reading this on. The requirement to reprogram it was **self-inflicted** by
choosing a route that does a modeset. 2po's conclusion ("write filtering is
closed") stands; its framing — that the display half therefore needs DCN 3.1.2
code — does not follow.

### The accelerator↔framebuffer bind ALREADY EXISTS — measured, not argued

`logs/20261022-222826-plugin/pci.txt`, an armed boot, on `.Display_boot`
(`class IONDRVFramebuffer`):

```
"IOFramebufferOpenGLIndex" = 0
"IOAccelRevision"          = 2
"IOAccelIndex"             = 0
"IOAccelTypes" = "IOService:/.../IGPU@0/AMDRadeonX6000_AMDNavi21GraphicsAccelerator"
```

and on the accelerator:

```
"IOAccelDisplayPipeCapabilities" = {"DisplayPipeSupported"=Yes,"TransactionsSupported"=Yes}
+-o IOAccelDisplayPipeUserClient2  ... "IOUserClientCreator" = "pid 162, WindowServer"
```

So: Apple's accelerator **found our IONDRVFramebuffer**, bound to it, published
the index triple on it, advertises display pipes AND transactions as supported,
and **WindowServer opened a display-pipe user client on it**. None of that was
known; all of it was sitting in a capture from the previous day.

Why it works is in the code, and there is no filtering anywhere:

- `IOAccelDisplayMachine::start(IOPCIDevice*)` runs two passes. Pass 1 walks
  the IOPCIDevice's children (`vtable[0x320]`, plane global at `0x14e7d0c0`),
  and for each asks `getClientWithCategory(OSSymbol("IOFramebuffer"))`
  (`vtable[0x420]`), casts the result to `IOFramebuffer` and calls
  `found_framebuffer` (`this->vtable[0x8d8]`). Pass 2 then **recursively walks
  the whole subtree** (`vtable[0x6a8]` child iterator) for anything that casts
  to `IOFramebuffer`, same call. `.Display_boot` is a direct child of the GPU's
  IOPCIDevice in category `IOFramebuffer`, so it is found by pass 1.
- `IOAccelDisplayMachine::found_framebuffer(IOFramebuffer*)` was disassembled
  in full. It checks for a duplicate, checks `count < accel->0xcb0` (a max),
  creates the pipe via `accel->vtable[0x908](fb)`, calls `find_vram_descriptor`
  and increments. **There is no class check, no provider check, no vendor
  check, no PCI-ID check.** Any `IOFramebuffer` is accepted.

This retires the theory this investigation started from — that
`SLSAcceleratorForDisplayNumber` finds no accelerator for our display. It
finds one. The keys it needs are present.

### The one call that defines the flippable window — and it is 8 MB

`IOGraphicsAccelerator2::find_vram_descriptor()` (0x14e53922), disassembled:

```
if (this->0x180) return true;                       // cached
for (i = 0; i < displayMachine->getFramebufferCount(); i++) {
    fb = displayMachine->getIOFramebuffer(i);
    if (!fb) continue;
    this->0x180 = fb->vtable[0x9b0]();              // <-- the whole input
    if (this->0x180) break;
}
if (!this->0x180) return false;
this->0x188 = desc->vtable[0x200](1);               // map
if (!this->0x188) { desc->release(); this->0x180 = 0; return false; }
this->0x190 = map->vtable[0x118]();                 // kernel VA
return true;
```

Slot `0x9b0` resolved against `__ZTV13IOFramebuffer` in IOGraphicsFamily:
**`IOFramebuffer::getVRAMRange()`**. Adjacent slot `0x9b8` is
`enableController` — the method 2pa already routes successfully, so this is a
proven-reachable region of this exact vtable.

**So the accelerator's entire notion of scanout VRAM is one virtual call, and
on this machine it returns 8294400 bytes — exactly one 1920x1080x4 buffer,
with room for zero others.**

That is the fourth and most consequential sense in which the "7 MB" is not
cosmetic. 2or said it was the label. 2pd said it indicates a CPU-mapped buffer
rather than a GPU surface. This says it is **the size of the window the
accelerator is permitted to flip inside** — and a flip needs a second buffer.
`bufferFlipCount = 0` and `bufferSwapCount = 0` in the same capture.

### It is routable

```
00000000150019a0 (__TEXT,__text) external __ZN17IONDRVFramebuffer12getVRAMRangeEv
```

Defined in IONDRVSupport, so rule 1 is satisfied. Rule 2: first bytes are
`55 / 48 89 e5 / 53` — push rbp, mov, push rbx — **no branch within the first
five bytes**; the first `je` is at +0x17. Routable.

Its body caches at `+0x238` and otherwise delegates to `vtable[0xc40]` =
**`IONDRVFramebuffer::findVRAM()`**, also defined in IONDRVSupport and
therefore also routable. `findVRAM` is where the value is born and it is
cached, so hooking it is a one-shot; `getVRAMRange` is what the accelerator
actually calls.

### What is measured and what is not — stated plainly

**Measured:** the bind exists; the index triple is published on
IONDRVFramebuffer; pipes and transactions are advertised; WindowServer holds a
pipe user client; `found_framebuffer` filters nothing; the accelerator's VRAM
descriptor comes from exactly one routable virtual; that virtual returns
8294400 bytes; flips and swaps are both 0; `ioSurfaceReadOutBytes = 40812544`
and `iosurfaceTextureCreationCount = 74`, i.e. WindowServer **is** making
GPU-backed IOSurfaces and reading ~40 MB back off the GPU.

**NOT measured — this is a hypothesis, not a result:** that the *reason* no
flip happens is the 8 MB. Competing explanations survive: the pipe's
`initFramebufferResource` may fail for an unrelated reason; SkyLight may build
its destination without consulting the display pipe at all; or a capability
distinct from the two advertised may be missing. 2pf's measurement
(`getDisplayPipeTransactionFlip` never called once) is consistent with all of
them.

What makes it worth one boot anyway is the risk profile, which is nothing like
2pk/2pm/2po: **no DCN register is written**, the hook is one return value on a
method Apple calls for information, it is gated behind a boot-arg, and the
failure mode is a wrong `IOFBMemorySize` rather than a dead pipe. The range
must start at the **same** physical base (BAR0 offset 0 / system-physical
`0x780000000`) and only be longer, so offset 0 remains the live scanout that
DCHUBBUB is already fetching — then even a total failure leaves the picture on
screen.

### Verdict on the user's question

**The accelerated framebuffer is not dead, and DCHUBBUB does not need to be
got past.** What is dead is making Apple's dcn302 DAL do a modeset (2po). The
display pipe is already built on our framebuffer, by Apple's own code, with
transactions advertised and a WindowServer client attached — four facts that
every milestone from 2oq onward assumed to be false.

## 2pq (2026-10-23) — the flip window, built to answer several questions in one boot

Built, not yet booted. `-rbgpufbvramrange`, default off.

### What it does

Routes `IONDRVFramebuffer::getVRAMRange()` (rule 1: defined in IONDRVSupport;
rule 2: `55 / 48 89 e5 / 53`, no branch in the first five bytes; rule 3:
grepped, not routed anywhere else; rule 5: both new mangled names taken from
`nm` output, not hand-written).

It does **not** answer blanket. `getVRAMRange` has **14 virtual call sites** —
IOGraphicsFamily 4, IOAcceleratorFamily2 6, IONDRVSupport 4 — and a blanket
change would also resize IOGraphics' aperture and `IOFBMemorySize`. It enlarges
for exactly **one return address**: the call inside
`IOGraphicsAccelerator2::find_vram_descriptor`, at that function `+0x4a`
(`ff 91 b0 09 00 00`, six bytes), so the return address is `+0x50`. Those six
bytes are **read back from the running kernel and compared** before anything is
enlarged; a mismatch logs the bytes it found and enlarges nothing. That is the
`mtlk` fail-safe pattern: an OS update that moves the call site means nothing
is patched rather than something wrong being patched.

The enlarged `IODeviceMemory` is built at the **same physical base as the
original**, read from the original object with `getPhysicalSegment(0, …)`
rather than hardcoded, and is only longer. Offset 0 therefore stays the live
scanout DCHUBBUB is already fetching, so even total failure leaves a picture.
Default 64 MB (8 buffers against the current 1), `rbgpufbvramrangemb=<N>`
clamped **8–256** because BAR0 is 256 MB — measured from `assigned-addresses`
on `IGPU@0`: `0x8_8000_0000`, length `0x1000_0000`. `find_vram_descriptor`
**maps the whole range**, so claiming more than the aperture would hand it a
range whose far end is not VRAM.

Reference convention checked rather than assumed: `getVRAMRange` returns a
**retained** reference (the original calls `retain()` before returning), so the
hook retains ours and **releases the original's**, which is not the one going
out.

Ordering: IONDRVSupport loads **before** IOAcceleratorFamily2, so the route is
armed before the call site is known. Until `processAccelFamily` resolves and
verifies it, the hook records callers and passes every call through untouched.

### Why one boot can answer more than one question

Rule 14, applied deliberately — and `-rbgpuflipprobe` is already routed and
observe-only (2pe/2pf), so the flip signal costs nothing extra.

| reading | where | what it settles |
|---|---|---|
| `fbvr_routed` | NVRAM | did the route land |
| `fbvr_verify` | NVRAM | did the six call-site bytes match |
| `fbvr_orig_len`, `fbvr_orig_base` | NVRAM / diag | **is it really 8294400, and at what base** — 2pp inferred this from `IOFBMemorySize`, a different call on a different node |
| `fbvr_hit` | NVRAM | did `find_vram_descriptor` actually ask |
| `fbvr_big` | NVRAM | did the enlarged range go out, how many times |
| `fbvr_fail` | NVRAM | 1 no original, 2 no base, 3 base unaligned, 4 already big, 5 `withRange` refused |
| `fbvr_calls`, `fbvr_ret1..8` | NVRAM / diag | **the whole caller set**, decoded against `kextstat` slides afterwards |
| `IOFBMemorySize` | `ioreg` | **control**: must stay 8294400, proving only the accelerator was affected |
| `bufferFlipCount`, `bufferSwapCount` | `ioreg` accel `PerformanceStatistics` | did flipping start |
| `fliprq` | `-rbgpuflipprobe` | did `getDisplayPipeTransactionFlip` fire — 2pf's zero is the control |
| `CompositorSW::CompositeLayersToDestination` | `sample WindowServer` | did software compositing drop from 48 % |
| nominal Hz | `tools/dispclk` | did 2oz/2ov regress |

The seven load-bearing keys are **first** in `kRbgpuNvramHotKeys`, so they
survive a boot with no usable screen (rule 10's reason, and the 512-byte budget
is spent frontier-first).

`fbvr_orig_len` is the gate on everything else: if it is not 8294400 the
machine was not in the state 2pp measured, and no other reading here means
anything.

### What a negative looks like, stated before the boot

`fbvr_hit ≥ 1` and `fbvr_big ≥ 1` with `bufferFlipCount` still 0 and `fliprq`
still never firing is a **clean negative**: the accelerator asked, got room for
eight buffers, and still did not flip — which kills the "no second buffer"
hypothesis outright and moves the question to `initFramebufferResource` or to
SkyLight's destination choice. Saying this now is what stops the boot being
spent twice.

`fbvr_hit = 0` says something different and equally useful: `find_vram_descriptor`
never ran again after our route armed, i.e. the accelerator cached its
descriptor before IONDRVSupport's hook existed — in which case the hook has to
move to `findVRAM` (also routable, also in IONDRVSupport) or earlier.

Build: imports **354/354** resolve via `IOPCIFamily` + `kpi.*` only — no
IOGraphicsFamily dependency (the 2oz trap), `IODeviceMemory::withRange`
resolves through `com.apple.kpi.iokit`. `hosttest: all passed`.
UUID `28BF4AC7-22A2-3EA5-B32A-3BB073908CCD`.

## 2pr (2026-10-23, boot 144) — the flip window was NOT the blocker, and SkyLight names the real one

`rbgpu-boot = 144` (rule 8: new, so the capture is this boot's). Boot-args
confirmed to hold `-rbgpufbvramrange` and **no** `-rbgpudal*` and no
`-rbgpuoff`, so 2pq armed alone — one new thing, not two.

### The hook did exactly what it was built to do

From the full `RBGPUDiag` table (decimal) and NVRAM (hex):

```
fbvr_routed    1            fbvr_verify    1
fbvr_orig_len  8294400      fbvr_orig_seg  8294400     (one contiguous segment)
fbvr_orig_base 36507222016  = 0x8_8000_0000            <-- BAR0's base, exactly
fbvr_biglen    67108864     = 64 MB                    built and handed over
fbvr_hit       2            fbvr_big       1
fbvr_fail      1            fbvr_calls     7
fbvr_ret1      = fbvr_callsite = fbvr_fvd + 0x50       <-- the intended site
```

So: the six call-site bytes verified, the gate passed (`8294400`), and
`fbvr_ret1` equals `fbvr_fvd + 0x50` by arithmetic — the hook fired at exactly
the one call inside `find_vram_descriptor` and nowhere else.

**`fbvr_orig_base = 0x880000000` is BAR0's base**, measured for the first time.
The GOP framebuffer *is* BAR0 offset 0, so the 64 MB range sat entirely inside
BAR0's 256 MB. The design assumption held, and that number is now known rather
than inferred.

**The control held.** `IOFBMemorySize` still reads **8294400** — the other 13
call sites got the original, so the change was surgical exactly as intended, and
nothing about IOGraphics' aperture moved. No regression anywhere: the vblank
reads nominal **133.801 Hz** / measured **137.04 Hz** (boot 138 was
129.267/134.10, so slightly better), and the desktop stayed up.

### And it changed nothing — the pre-stated clean negative

`bufferFlipCount = 0`. `bufferSwapCount = 0`. `fliprq_routed = 1` with **no
`fliprq_calls`**, so `getDisplayPipeTransactionFlip` was never called, exactly
as in 2pf.

2pq wrote down in advance what this would mean, so it cannot be relitigated:
*"`fbvr_hit ≥ 1` and `fbvr_big ≥ 1` with `bufferFlipCount` still 0 … is a clean
negative"*. That is what happened. **Room was not what was missing.** The
accelerator was handed eight buffers' worth of scanout VRAM, accepted it, and
still never asked for a flip.

`fbvr_fail = 1` is worth naming rather than hiding: `find_vram_descriptor`'s
**first** call got NULL from `getVRAMRange` (IONDRVFramebuffer returns 0 until
`0x218` is set and `0x238` is cached — pre-existing behaviour we did not cause),
and its second call got our 64 MB. So the enlarged descriptor *is* what
`accel->0x180` ends up holding. Whether a consumer read `0x180` between the two
calls is not observable from this hook, and is the one thread this boot leaves
loose.

### The sample proves nothing, and saying so is the point

`CompositorSW` lines: **0**. `CA::OGL::SW` lines: **0**. `CompositorMetal`:
2. That looks like the fix. **It is not evidence.** The sample was 3 seconds on
an idle desktop: **2370 of 2371 main-thread samples were in `mach_msg`**, and
the single composite frame was `CaptureSurfaceMetal::Populate` — a *capture*
surface, not the display destination. 2pd's 48 % was measured under load. n=1
(rule 18). Nothing about the display composite path changed measurably here.

### SkyLight names the defect itself — and it predates 2pq

The unified log, which no previous milestone had read with this predicate:

```
WindowServer[161] [com.apple.SkyLight:default] Unsupported sw composite destination.
```

**31 299 times in boot 144's 45 minutes.** And in boot 143's window
(10:00–10:45, before `-rbgpufbvramrange` existed at all): **46 994 times.** So
it is **pre-existing**, not caused by the hook — attribution clean (rule 16).

This is a far better handle than anything the display half has had. SkyLight is
not silently choosing software compositing; it is **rejecting the destination
outright, by name, tens of thousands of times a boot**. Two sibling strings sit
beside it in SkyLight:

```
Unexpected composite destination type (%d)
Unreasonable composite destination bounds requested: (%.1f, %.1f) [%.1f x ...
```

The first would print the destination **type as a number** — the single most
useful value available — and it has **never fired**, so our destination does not
reach that path. `Metal compositor activated.` is still logged (11:23:46), which
is consistent with 2pd: the Metal compositor is activated and the *display
destination* is what it cannot take.

### What this closes and what it opens

**CLOSED: the flip window.** The accelerator's scanout VRAM size is not the
blocker. 2pp's finding that the bind, the pipe and the WindowServer client all
already exist stands and is now strengthened — every structural precondition is
present and the thing that fails is the **destination object itself**, in
userspace, in SkyLight.

**OPEN, and the new frontier:** what makes a destination "supported". The
answer is in SkyLight, which `dyld_info` can read out of the cache
(`/System/Cryptexes/OS/System/Library/dyld/dyld_shared_cache_x86_64h`), and the
work is to find the function emitting that string and the predicate it tests.
That is static, costs no boot, and is where the next effort belongs — not in
another kernel hook.

### Instrument bugs this boot exposed (rule 16: the instrument is a suspect)

Three, all mine, all fixed in `tools/fbvr_check.sh`:

1. **The script read only NVRAM**, which holds the hot keys alone, so **11 of 18
   `fbvr_*` keys were invisible** — including `fbvr_orig_base`, `fbvr_biglen`,
   `fbvr_fvd` and `fbvr_ret1..8`. The full table is `RBGPUDiag` in the
   IORegistry and was readable the whole time.
2. **It compared a HEX diag value against a DECIMAL constant.** NVRAM printed
   `fbvr_orig_len=7e9000`; the guidance line said "8294400 = the state 2pp
   measured". `0x7e9000 == 8294400`. The gate had **passed** and the report made
   it look like it failed.
3. **The flip-probe grep used the wrong key names** (`^flip|^fliprq` against
   NVRAM, where they never were). The real keys are `fliprq_on` /
   `fliprq_routed` / `fliprq_calls` in the registry — rule 26 again, fourth time
   this project.

## 2ps (2026-10-23) — the SkyLight predicate, read. Zero boots.

2pr found SkyLight rejecting the display destination by name ~47 000 times a
boot. This reads the code that does it.

### New capability: `tools/re/dsc.py`

The dyld shared cache cannot be turned into a standalone Mach-O with anything
on this machine - there is no `otool` that will open a cache-resident path
(`otool-classic: can't open file`), `llvm-objdump` has **no `-b binary`**,
there is no `llvm-mc`, and `capstone` is not installed. So the tool does three
things directly:

- parses the cache header's mappings for **VA <-> file offset** (map0: VA
  `0x7ff800000000`, fileoff 0, size `0x25198000`, r-x)
- finds **RIP-relative LEA cross-references** to an address, using
  `bytes.find` per 3-byte opcode prefix (REX.W `48`/`4C` + `8D` + modrm
  mod=00 rm=101) so all 622 MB of the r-x mapping scans in seconds
- wraps raw bytes in a **minimal x86-64 MH_OBJECT** with one `__TEXT,__text`
  section at the right vmaddr, so `objdump -d` disassembles cache-resident
  code at correct addresses

`dyld_info -segments` supplies an image's unslid base: SkyLight `__TEXT` =
**`0x7FF807B42000`**, 4923 KB.

### Rule 26, paid again, and the control is what saved it

The first xref returned **0 sites** - and that was my arithmetic, not absence.
I wrote the string's VA as `0x7FDF8F0` when file offset 134092464 is
`0x7FE1670`: **off by 8128 bytes**. Dumping the bytes at the wrong VA showed
unrelated strings ("connection for the requested process is null"), which is
what exposed it, after a **known-present control** - "Metal compositor
activated", which has exactly one LEA xref at `0x7ff807c9a87b` - proved the
pipeline itself was sound. Without that control I would have reported "the
string is never referenced", confidently and wrongly, which is exactly the
failure rule 26 exists for.

Corrected: the string is at **`0x7ff807fe16b0`** (verified by dumping it:
`Unsupported sw composite destination.` + NUL) with **exactly one** LEA xref at
`0x7ff807c3eb9a`, into `rcx`, feeding the standard
`_os_log_impl(dso=0x7ff807b42000, log, type=0x10 = ERROR, fmt, buf, size)`.

### The predicate, exactly

The function begins at **`0x7ff807c3e820`** and takes the source in `rsi` and
the **destination in `rdx`**. Exactly **one** branch reaches the error block at
`0x7ff807c3eb68`:

```
7ff807c3e83f:  testq %rsi, %rsi
7ff807c3e842:  je    ...                  ; no source -> out
7ff807c3e848:  movq  %rdx, %rbx           ; rbx = destination
7ff807c3e84b:  movl  0x2c(%rdx), %eax
7ff807c3e84e:  cmpl  0x34(%rdx), %eax
7ff807c3e851:  jg    ...                  ; bounds: 0x2c must be <= 0x34
7ff807c3e857:  movl  0x30(%rbx), %eax
7ff807c3e85a:  cmpl  0x38(%rbx), %eax
7ff807c3e85d:  jg    ...                  ; bounds: 0x30 must be <= 0x38
7ff807c3e866:  movl  0x10(%rbx), %r13d    ; <<< destination TYPE, int32 at +0x10
7ff807c3e86a:  cmpl  $0x2, %r13d
7ff807c3e86e:  je    0x7ff807c3e896       ; type 2 -> OK, uses dest->0x98
7ff807c3e870:  cmpl  $0x1, %r13d
7ff807c3e874:  jne   0x7ff807c3eb68       ; <<< NOT 1 AND NOT 2 -> REJECT
7ff807c3e87a:  movq  0x18(%rbx), %rax     ; type 1 -> OK, uses dest->0x18
```

**The gate is a single int32 at destination+0x10, and it must be 1 or 2.**
Type 1 is served out of `dest->0x18`, type 2 out of `dest->0x98`. This is the
mechanical form of what 2pd inferred from the two constructors it named.

The sibling errors - `Unexpected composite destination type (%d)`
(`0x7ff807fe40f0`) and `Unreasonable composite destination bounds requested`
(`0x7ff807fe4090`) - are both emitted from one other function, around
`0x7ff807cbf900`, and **neither has ever fired**, so our destination does not
reach that path. The one that would have printed the type number is the one
that stays silent.

No `WSCompositeDestination*` symbol is **exported** from SkyLight, so the
constructors are internal and cannot be found by name.

### Where the type is assigned - and what is NOT yet known

Scanning SkyLight's `__text` for `movl $imm, 0x10(reg)` with imm < 16 found a
coherent small group writing the type field:

| value | sites |
|---|---|
| 2 | `0x7ff807c6e5c0`, `0x7ff807ccff97` |
| 3 | `0x7ff807c97f1f`, `0x7ff807f275ba` |

(The ad-hoc scan labelled these `%rsi`; the type-3 site is actually
`41 c7 46 10 03…` = `movl $0x3, 0x10(%r14)`, because a REX.B prefix precedes
it and the throwaway scanner did not decode REX. The offset and the immediate
are right; the register name in that one listing is not.)

`0x7ff807c6e5c0` writes **2** into a structure it has just zeroed with a run of
`movaps`, then sets `0x80` = 4 and two floats - a freshly constructed
destination. The type-**3** site sets `0x18`, `0x20`, a byte at `0x28`, zeroes
`0x30` and `0x48`, writes `3` to `0x10`, and then branches on whether `0x18` is
null - so **type 3 also populates the `0x18` field that the accepted type 1
uses.**

**What is NOT established, and must not be assumed: that our destination is
type 3.** Three values are now known to exist (1, 2, 3) and the predicate
accepts two of them, but nothing measured here says which one the display gets.
The structural similarity between 1 and 3 is suggestive and is *not* evidence.

### The two ways to get the actual value, and their cost

1. **Static**: keep going - find which constructor the display path calls. Free,
   and the next thing to try.
2. **Runtime**: read `dest->0x10` in WindowServer. WindowServer is a platform
   binary and strips `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES`, so injection cannot reach it -
   but **the kernel-side patcher already does** (2og/2oi/2on,
   `-rbgpumtlkfix`), which patches the dyld cache per-process for ~2045 execs
   per boot including Safari and WindowServer, verifying every site from the
   target's own memory first. The mechanism for a SkyLight detour therefore
   already exists and is proven. Costs a boot, and should not be spent until
   the static route is exhausted.

**Do not patch the predicate to accept 3 as a "fix".** It would make the SW
compositor read `dest->0x18` on a structure whose `0x18` has not been shown to
mean the same thing, inside WindowServer, which is the one process whose crash
takes the desktop with it.

## 2pt (2026-10-23) — the function is confirmed, and 2pr's headline was WRONG

Zero boots. Symbolized, which 2ps could not do, and the symbols overturn 2pr's
central claim.

### How to symbolize SkyLight without root (reusable)

`atos` cannot take a cache-resident path, and WindowServer needs root. But the
dyld cache slide is **per-boot and system-wide**, so any process that loads
SkyLight has it at the same address:

```
python3 -c "import ctypes,os,time; ctypes.CDLL('/System/Library/PrivateFrameworks/SkyLight.framework/SkyLight'); ..."
vmmap <pid> | grep SkyLight        # __TEXT base
atos -p <pid> <unslid + (base - 0x7FF807B42000)>
```

`vmmap` reports `__TEXT 4924K`, matching `dyld_info`'s 4923 KB on the unslid
base `0x7FF807B42000` — an independent check that the base is right.

**The slide must be MEASURED, not carried over.** The first attempt reused the
slide computed from boot 144's `sample` file (`0x2CE7000`) and `atos` answered
`libBLAS.dylib` for every address. The machine had **rebooted** —
`uptime: up 23 mins` — and `rbgpu-boot` still read **144** because `rbgpu-arm`
is one-shot (rule 9), so the stale counter hid a whole new boot. Rule 8 caught
it. In this boot the slide is `0x8052000`.

### Confirmed: the function with the type gate is CompositorSW

```
0x7ff807c3e820 -> CompositorSW::CompositeLayersToDestination(
                      WSCompositeSourceLayer*, WSCompositeDestination*,
                      unsigned long long) + 0
0x7ff807ef5c94 -> CompositorMetal::CompositeLayersToDestination(...) + 0
0x7ff807cbf900 -> MetalContext::StartComposite(WSCompositeDestination*,
                      MTLLoadAction, MTLStoreAction) + 1096
```

So 2ps's predicate is exactly `CompositorSW::CompositeLayersToDestination`'s —
**the same function 2pd measured at 48 % of WindowServer's main thread** — and
its gate is `dest->type` (int32 at +0x10) ∈ {1, 2}. That part stands.

### And here is the correction

**`0x7ff807c97e47` = `SLDisplayStreamCreateCommon`.** The type-**3** write at
`0x7ff807c97f1f` is inside *display-stream* creation — `CGDisplayStream`, i.e.
**screen capture**, not the display scanout. The other sites the `setimm` scan
turned up resolve to `_CGXSetMenuBar`, `SLSSetMenuBar` and
`FanPolygon::FanPolygon(CGPath const*)`, which are **unrelated structures that
merely have an int at +0x10**. So 2ps's "three type values are now known to
exist — 1, 2 and 3" was over-claimed: the scan was not type-aware, and the only
value tied to a real `WSCompositeDestination` is **3 = a display stream**.

**2pr's headline is wrong.** It said the rejection *"predates every display
hook and is the real blocker"*. Two things kill that:

1. **I had no unarmed control.** 2pr compared boot 143 (46 994 rejections) with
   boot 144 (31 299) — **both armed, both with every display hook active** —
   and generalized to "predates every display hook". On the boot this was
   written in, with the display hooks running (`dispclk` nominal **131.671 Hz**,
   measured **134.07 Hz**, so the vblank path is live), the count over 20
   minutes is **1**. Note `rbgpu-arm` being absent does **not** disable the
   hooks — it only gates the NVRAM/diag capture — so this is a genuine
   hooks-on comparison. 47 000 versus 1 tracks **machine activity**, not our
   code.
2. **CompositorSW accepts the display's destination.** 2pd measured
   `CompositorSW::CompositeLayersToDestination` burning 48 % of the main thread
   doing real work through `CA::OGL::SW::`. A destination it *rejects* costs
   nothing — the `jne` goes straight to the epilogue. So the display
   destination's type **is** 1 or 2 and is perfectly acceptable to CompositorSW.
   That is precisely *why* the desktop composites in software.

Putting both together: the rejection is about **display streams** (type 3,
`SLDisplayStreamCreateCommon`), which is some screen-capture client, and it is
**not the display defect**. It was log noise that looked like a smoking gun
because it was loud, named and sat next to the right layer.

### Where this leaves the display question

Back where 2pd put it, with one thing now firmly established rather than
inferred: **the display destination is one CompositorSW can take, and the
question is why the composite goes to CompositorSW rather than
CompositorMetal.** `MetalContext::StartComposite(WSCompositeDestination*, ...)`
is the Metal side's entry and is named; the per-composite choice between the
two compositors is the thing to read next, not the destination's validity.

The honest summary of 2pr -> 2pt: a loud log line is not a diagnosis, and
"predates X" needs a boot where X is off before it can be said at all.

## 2pu (2026-10-23) — THE COMPOSITOR SELECTION, NAMED END TO END. Zero boots.

2pt left the right question: why does the display composite go to
`CompositorSW` when the log says `Metal compositor activated.`? This answers it,
and the answer is two concrete values, not a missing driver.

### The chain, every link symbolized

The caller stack came from a **spindump already on disk**
(`logs/20261019-003554-metal/ws-spindump.txt`) - measured, not inferred:

```
WS::Updater::UpdateDisplays(CGXConnection*, bool, vector<shared_ptr<WS::Displays::Display>>)
  -> WS::Displays::CDDisplay::render_update(WS::Displays::Update&, Compositor*,
                                            unsigned int, WSCompositeSourceLayer*)
    -> CompositorSW::CompositeLayersToDestination(...)        <- 2pd's 48 %
```

`render_update` **takes the `Compositor*` as an argument**, so the display does
not choose it - its caller does. At the call site
(`UpdateDisplays + 20990`, unslid `0x7ff807e337e3`):

```
movq -0xa00(%rbp), %rdx     ; the Compositor*
leaq -0x510(%rbp), %rsi     ; &Update
movl %ebx, %ecx
callq *0x4f8(%rax)          ; virtual render_update, display vtable slot +0x4f8
```

and the display's own accessor, `WS::Displays::CDDisplay::compositor() const`
(unslid `0x7ff807d6c13c`), is four instructions:

```
movq (%rdi), %rax
callq *0x60(%rax)           ; virtual: the display's ACCELERATOR ID -> edi
movl %eax, %edi
jmp  0x7ff807c9b78c         ; tail call WSGetCompositorForAccelerator
```

### The decision, exactly

`WSGetCompositorForAccelerator(unsigned int accelId)`, unslid `0x7ff807c9b78c`:

```
mode = *0x7ff843c9ecdc                       ; 0 = Metal, 1 = SW, 2 = debug
if (mode == 2)                 return *0x7ff843c9eca0;   ; debug singleton
if (mode != 0)                 return *0x7ff843c9eca8;   ; SW singleton
;  ---- mode == 0, i.e. "Metal compositor activated." ----
if (accelId == 0)              return *0x7ff843c9eca8;   ; <<< SOFTWARE
if ((*0x7ff843ca08b0 & 1) == 0) return *0x7ff843c9eca8;  ; <<< SOFTWARE
return getMetalCompositorFor(accelId);                   ; 0x7ff807c99cd6
```

The mode global was pinned down from the activators, which the log strings
locate: `activate_compositor_metal(bool)` (`0x7ff807c9a826`) writes **0**,
`activate_compositor_sw(bool)` (`0x7ff807c9a8ae`) writes **1**, and
`WSCompositorSetDebugOptions` writes **2**. `activate_compositor_default()` and
`WSGetCompositorForAccelerator` are the readers that matter; the rest are
`set_debug_options` and `DumpWSCDIOPWSAA`.

**So: Metal IS activated globally, and the display is still handed the software
compositor, by one of exactly two tests** - `accelId == 0`, or bit 0 of the flag
at `0x7ff843ca08b0` being clear. Nothing else in that function can produce the
SW singleton once mode is 0.

The other eight callers confirm the shape - `displaystream_update`,
`device_composite_windows`, `WindowFreeze::Update`, `WSCALayerBacking::Flatten`,
`WSCALayerBacking::BeginUpdate`, `CaptureSurface::PrepareForPopulation`,
`WSCompositeWindowToDestination` - every consumer gets its compositor from this
one selector, per accelerator.

### What this changes

The display half has been framed since 2oq as "macOS has no DCN 3.1.2 code, so
the destination can never be a GPU surface". 2pt already removed the
destination from the story (CompositorSW **accepts** it). This removes the
driver from the story too: **the software path is chosen by an `if` on two
integers, before any destination or driver capability is consulted.**

### The one thing NOT established

**Which of the two tests fails, and what `accelId` actually is.** It comes from
a virtual method at the display's vtable slot **+0x60**, and naming that needs
the vtable, whose slots in `__DATA_CONST` are **chained-fixup encoded** - slot
`+0x60` of CDDisplay's vtable (address point `0x7ff88166da20`, found by locating
`render_update`'s raw pointer at `0x7ff88166df18` and subtracting `0x4f8`) reads
`0x10e017c79de`, which is an encoding, not an address. Decoding chained fixups
is the next piece of tooling.

A correction while here: 2pt's remark that the compositor vtable region
"interleaves non-pointer values, so it isn't a plain vtable" was wrong about the
cause. Those values are **chained-fixup encodings** of the slots that need
rebasing; the ones that symbolized cleanly happen to be stored raw. It is a
vtable.

**And a trap to avoid naming it too fast:** 2pp measured `IOAccelIndex = 0` on
our `IONDRVFramebuffer`, which is tempting to equate with `accelId == 0`. But a
normal single-GPU Mac also has `IOAccelIndex = 0` and composites with Metal, so
either 0 is a legal id there and our problem is the capability flag, or `accelId`
is a different number entirely. **Do not report IOAccelIndex as the cause
without reading slot +0x60.**

### Why the next step is cheap either way

Both values are readable at runtime, and both are plain integers:

- the flag at `0x7ff843ca08b0` and the mode at `0x7ff843c9ecdc` are **globals in
  SkyLight's `__DATA`**, so any process that loads SkyLight has them at
  `unslid + slide` - no root, no WindowServer, no boot. The flag's writer is
  inside a `dispatch_once` block, so its value is only knowable by reading it.
- `accelId` needs the display, i.e. WindowServer - but the kernel-side patcher
  (2og/2oi/2on) already reaches WindowServer and verifies every site from the
  target's own memory first.

Read the two globals from a scratch process first. That is free and it halves
the question.

---

## 2pv (2026-10-23) — deduced: the display gets the software compositor because its ACCELERATOR ID IS 0

Zero boots. 2pu left two candidate causes; this eliminates one of them by
exhaustive static analysis plus one measured log line.

### The elimination

`activate_compositor_default()` is at unslid `0x7ff807c9abe1`:

```
7ff807c9abf9:  cmpb $0x0, *0x7ff843c9ed28     ; the "force software" byte
7ff807c9ac00:  je   -> activate_compositor_metal
7ff807c9ac05:  jmp     activate_compositor_sw(false)
```

So **Metal is activated if and only if `*0x7ff843c9ed28 == 0`.**

That byte has, across the whole of SkyLight's `__text`, **exactly one writer and
exactly one reader**:

```
7ff807c9abf9:  cmpb $0x0, 0x7ff843c9ed28      ; the read, above
7ff807c9ac4f:  movb $0x1, 0x7ff843c9ed28      ; the ONLY write
```

and that single write sits behind:

```
7ff807c9ac46:  cmpb $0x0, *0x7ff843ca08b0     ; the Metal-capability flag
7ff807c9ac4d:  jne  -> return                 ; capable -> leave the byte 0
7ff807c9ac4f:  movb $0x1, *0x7ff843c9ed28     ; NOT capable -> force software
```

A `static` byte starts at 0, so `*0x7ff843c9ed28 != 0` is reachable **only**
through the capability flag reading zero.

**Measured**: the unified log on this machine says
`[com.apple.SkyLight:default] Metal compositor activated.`, and that string has
**exactly one** LEA cross-reference in the entire cache — inside
`activate_compositor_metal` (2ps). So that function ran.

Therefore `*0x7ff843c9ed28 == 0`, therefore the capability flag
`*0x7ff843ca08b0` is **non-zero**. It is handled everywhere as a boolean
(`andb $0x1`, `cmpb $0x1`), so non-zero means bit 0 is set.

### The conclusion

In `WSGetCompositorForAccelerator` (2pu), with mode `== 0`:

```
if (accelId == 0)               return SW singleton;   <-- the only one left
if ((*0x7ff843ca08b0 & 1) == 0) return SW singleton;   <-- CANNOT fire, just proved
return getMetalCompositorFor(accelId);
```

**The display is handed `CompositorSW` because the accelerator id it reports is
0.** Not because of a destination type, not because of a missing capability, and
not because macOS lacks DCN 3.1.2 code. One integer, read from the display's own
virtual method at vtable slot **+0x60**, is zero.

### What that integer is NOT

**It is not simply `IOAccelIndex`.** 2pp measured `IOAccelIndex = 0` on our
`.Display_boot`, which is the obvious match and is almost certainly wrong: an
ordinary single-GPU Mac also publishes `IOAccelIndex = 0` and composites its
primary display with Metal. If `accelId == 0` meant software there too, Metal
display compositing would never happen on any Mac. So **0 is the "no accelerator
resolved" value**, and the real numbering is something else — an id or handle
that is 1-based or table-allocated. Writing `IOAccelIndex = 1` and hoping is
exactly the kind of move that costs a boot and teaches nothing.

### Next, and still free

Name the method at CDDisplay's vtable slot `+0x60`. The vtable's address point
is `0x7ff88166da20` (located by finding `CDDisplay::render_update`'s raw pointer
at `0x7ff88166df18` and subtracting the `+0x4f8` call offset), and slot `+0x60`
reads `0x10e017c79de`, which is a **chained-fixup encoding**, not an address.
Decoding the cache's chained fixups is the missing piece of `tools/re/dsc.py`;
once slot `+0x60` has a name, what feeds it can be read directly, and only then
is it worth spending a boot.

`SLSAcceleratorForDisplayNumber` (unslid `0x7FF807E0C67C`; export offsets are
image-relative, verified with `atos`) is a nearby public entry with signature
`(uint displayNumber, uint *out, uint *out2)` that zeroes both outputs before
looking anything up — a plausible sibling of the same lookup, and readable.

### Correcting 2pu

2pu ended by saying the mode and capability globals could be read from a scratch
process for free and that this would halve the question. **That was wrong**:
both are initialised at runtime (the capability behind a `dispatch_once`), so a
process that merely dlopens SkyLight shows static defaults, not WindowServer's
values. The deduction above replaced that plan and is stronger, because it rests
on a log line the machine actually emitted plus a single-writer proof rather than
on a value read out of the wrong process.

---

## 2pw (2026-10-23) — the chain is complete: CoreDisplay does not give our display an accelerator

Zero boots. Slot `+0x60` is named, and the path runs out of SkyLight entirely.

### Two corrections first, both mine

**1. `tools/re/dsc.py` could not see vtables at all, and 2pu/2pv said the wrong
thing about why.** Parsing the cache's `mappingWithSlideOffset` (header `0x138`)
shows which mappings carry slide info:

```
map0 va 0x7ff800000000 (__TEXT)      slideInfo 0        -> contents LITERAL
map1 va 0x7ff840000000 (__DATA_CONST) slideInfo v2      -> contents ENCODED
map2 va 0x7ff843670000               slideInfo v2       -> contents ENCODED
map3 va 0x7ff880000000               slideInfo 0        -> contents LITERAL
```

v2 parameters for both encoded mappings: `delta_mask 0x00ffff0000000000`
(shift 40), `value_add 0x7ff800000000`, so a slot's target is
`(value & ~delta_mask) + value_add`.

**Vtables live in `__DATA_CONST` (map1), which is encoded** — which is why a raw
byte search for `CDDisplay::render_update`'s pointer never found a vtable. What
it *did* find, at `0x7ff88166df18` in map3, was a **symbol table**: dumping that
region shows it strictly alternating a real text pointer with a monotonically
increasing value (`+0x26`, `+0x2d`, `+0x2e`…), i.e. (function address, name
string offset). So 2pu/2pv's "slot +0x60 reads `0x10e017c79de`, a chained-fixup
encoding" was wrong twice over: that region is not a vtable, and the value is a
string offset, not an encoded pointer. The `- 0x4f8` arithmetic on it was
meaningless.

With v2 decoding added (`dsc.py slide` / `dataxref` / `rdptr`), the real vtable
slot for `render_update` is **`0x7ff840a57eb8`**, giving address point
`0x7ff840a579c0` — and the header checks out, `offset-to-top` and the typeinfo
slot both zero at `-0x10`/`-0x8`.

### Slot +0x60, and the whole path

```
0x7ff807d699ee  WS::Displays::CDDisplay::vendor() const
0x7ff807d69a06  WS::Displays::CDDisplay::model() const
0x7ff807d69b10  WS::Displays::CDDisplay::accelerator() const     <- slot +0x60
```

```
CDDisplay::accelerator():
    rdi = this->0x158
    if (rdi == NULL) return 0
    tail jmp CGXGLDisplayDeviceAccelerator

CGXGLDisplayDeviceAccelerator(device):                   [SkyLight 0x7ff807dd86bf]
    if (*0x7ff843c9ecd8 == 1) { ...legacy path... }
    if (!WSMetalCompositorEnabled())            -> 0     ; 0x7ff807c9ac71
    CGXAcceleratorForDisplayDevice(device, -1, &id)      ; CoreDisplay
    if (id == 0)                                -> 0     ; <<< the failure
    ...
    return id

CGXAcceleratorForDisplayDevice(device, ...):   [CoreDisplay 0x7ff8041291df unslid]
    if (device == NULL) return 0x3e9            ; 1001
    jmp *(device->0x8)->0x148                   ; per-device ops entry
```

`WSMetalCompositorEnabled` is the predicate 2pv proved true on this machine
(`mode == 0 && (capability & 1)`), so that gate passes. The remaining way to get
0 is `CGXAcceleratorForDisplayDevice` returning 0.

### So the whole thing, end to end

```
UpdateDisplays
 -> CDDisplay::compositor()
     -> CDDisplay::accelerator()              [vtable +0x60]
         -> CGXGLDisplayDeviceAccelerator
             -> WSMetalCompositorEnabled()            PASSES (2pv)
             -> CGXAcceleratorForDisplayDevice        returns 0  <<<<
 -> WSGetCompositorForAccelerator(0)
     -> CompositorSW                                  the 48 % (2pd)
```

**The display composites in software because CoreDisplay does not associate an
accelerator with our display device.** Not a destination type (2pt), not a
missing SkyLight capability (2pv), not the flip window (2pr), and not - at this
layer - the absence of DCN 3.1.2 code.

### `IOAccelIndex` is definitively NOT the input

2pv flagged the temptation; this settles it. The id does not come from a
framebuffer property at all - it comes from a **function pointer at
`(device->0x8)->0x148`**, a per-device-type ops entry inside CoreDisplay. So
nothing we publish on `IONDRVFramebuffer` can change it directly, and the 2pp
reading of `IOAccelIndex = 0` is unrelated to this zero.

### Next, and it is a real question rather than a guess

Which ops table our display device gets, and what that `+0x148` entry does.
That is CoreDisplay, same technique, no boots: the cache is readable, the slide
is measurable, `atos` names things through a scratch process. The honest
expectation to set: CoreDisplay deciding "this display has no accelerator" may
well be downstream of the display being an `IONDRVFramebuffer` rather than an
accelerated framebuffer - in which case this chain ends up pointing back at the
same large body of work, but it will do so **with the exact predicate named**
instead of inferred, which is worth having either way.
